title: The power of the apostles’ words
source_text: Ἀλλὰ τὴν μὲν τάξιν καὶ σύνθεσιν καὶ φράσιν τῶν ἀπὸ φιλοσοφίας λόγων τοιαῦτα εἰς τοὺς προειρημένους πεποιηκέναι. καὶ ἄλλως κακῶς βεβιωκότας. οὐ πάνυ τι θαυμαστόν. ἐπὰν δὲ οὕς φησιν εἶναι ἰδιωτικοὺς λόγους ὁ Κέλσος κατανοήσωμεν, ὡσπερεὶ ἐπῳδὰς δυνάμεως πεπληρωμένους, καὶ τοὺς λόγους θεωρῶμεν, ἀθρόως προτρέποντας πλήθη ἐπὶ τὸν ἐξ ἀκολάστων εἰς τὸν εὐσταθέστατον βίον καὶ τὸν ἐξ ἀδίκων εἰς τὸν χρηστότερον καὶ τὸν ἐκ δειλῶν ἢ ἀνάνδρων εἰς τὸν ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον εὔτονον, ὡς καὶ θανάτου διὰ τὴν φανεῖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς εὐσέβειαν καταφρονεῖν· πῶς οὐχὶ δικαίως θαυμάσομεν τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ δύναμιν; „ὁ“ γὰρ „λόγος“ τῶν ταῦτα τὴν ἀρχὴν πρεσβευσάντων καὶ καμόντων, ἵνα συστήσωσιν ἐκκλησίας θεοῦ. ἀλλὰ καὶ „τὸ κήρυγμα“ αὐτῶν ἐν πειθοῖ μὲν γέγονεν οὐ τοιαύτῃ δὲ, ὁποία ἐστὶ πειθὼ ἐν τοῖς σοφίαν Πλάτωνος ἐπαγγελλομένοις ἤ τινος τῶν φιλοσοφησάντων. ὄντων ἀνθρώπων καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως ἐχόντων· ἡ δ᾿ ἀπόδειξις ἐν τοῖς Ἰησοῦ ἀποστόλοις θεόθεν δοθεῖσα πιστικὴ ἀπὸ „πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως.“ διόπερ τάχιστα καὶ ὀξύτατα ἔδραμεν ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν, μᾶλλον δὲ ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ, δι᾿ αὐτῶν μεταβάλλων πολλοὺς τῶν ἁμαρτάνειν πεφυκότων καὶ εἰθισμένων· οὓς οὐδὲ κολάζων μὲν ἄν τις ἄνθρωπος μετέβαλεν, ὁ δὲ λόγος μετεποίησε μορφώσας καὶ τυπώσας αὐτοὺς κατὰ τὸ αὐτοῦ βούλημα.
pass_a_gloss: But that the order (τάξις) and composition (σύνθεσις) and diction (φράσις) of the discourses from philosophy made such things toward those mentioned before, and others who had lived badly, is not at all wonderful (θαυμαστός). But when we consider (κατανοέω) the discourses which Celsus says are unlearned (ἰδιωτικός), as it were charms (ἐπῳδή) filled (πληρόω) with power (δύναμις), and observe (θεωρέω) the discourses exhorting (προτρέπω) multitudes (πλῆθος) all at once (ἀθρόως) toward the life out of licentious (ἀκόλαστος) into the most stable (εὐσταθέστατος), and out of unjust into the better (χρηστότερος), and out of cowardly (δειλός) or unmanly (ἄνανδρος) into the one so firm (εὔτονος) as even to despise (καταφρονέω) death because of the piety (εὐσέβεια) that appeared (φαίνω, aor. pass.) in them: how shall we not justly marvel at the power in it? For 'the word' of those who at the beginning (τὴν ἀρχήν) were ambassadors (πρεσβεύω) of these things and laboured (κάμνω) that they might establish (συνίστημι) churches (ἐκκλησία) of God; but also their 'preaching' (κήρυγμα) came to be in persuasion (πειθώ), but not such as is the persuasion in those professing (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) the wisdom (σοφία) of Plato or of any of those who philosophised, being men and having nothing else except human nature; but the demonstration (ἀπόδειξις) in the apostles of Jesus, given from God (θεόθεν), persuasive (πιστικός) from 'Spirit and power'. Therefore most swiftly and most keenly (ὀξύτατα) ran (τρέχω, aor. ἔδραμον) their word, or rather that of God, through them changing (μεταβάλλω) many of those by nature sinning and accustomed; whom not even punishing would any human being have changed, but the Word remade (μεταποιέω), forming (μορφόω) and moulding (τυπόω) them according to his will (βούλημα).
pass_b_english: Still, that the order, composition and style of philosophical discourses should have done such things for the men just named and for others who had lived badly is not very surprising. But when we consider the words that Celsus calls unlearned, filled with power as though they were charms, and observe those words urging whole multitudes at once to pass from licentiousness to the steadiest of lives, from injustice to a better life, and from cowardice or unmanliness to such firmness that they despise even death because of the piety that has shown itself in them, how shall we not rightly marvel at the power within it?

For "the word" of those who first served as ambassadors of these things and laboured to found churches of God, and their "preaching" as well, came with persuasion, but not the kind of persuasion found in those who profess the wisdom of Plato or of any other philosopher, men who had nothing beyond human nature. But the demonstration given by God in the apostles of Jesus was persuasive, coming "from the Spirit and power" (1 Corinthians 2:4). That is why their word, or rather the Word of God, ran with the utmost speed and keenness, changing through them many of those naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it. No human being could have changed them, not even by punishing them; but the Word remade them, forming and shaping them according to his own will.

choices.choice: 1 Corinthians 2:4: ὁ λόγος μου καὶ τὸ κήρυγμά μου οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖ σοφίας λόγοις ἀλλ' ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως. Origen weaves Paul's words 'the word', 'the preaching', 'persuasion', 'demonstration', 'Spirit and power' into his own sentence; only the marked phrases (ὁ λόγος, τὸ κήρυγμα, πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως) are put in quotation marks, as in the edition, and the single citation follows the last of them. The first sentence of the second paragraph lacks a main verb for ὁ λόγος in the Greek; it is supplied from γέγονεν ('came with persuasion'). The TEI full stops after πεποιηκέναι and βεβιωκότας, and after φιλοσοφησάντων, break single sentences; read as continuous. προτρέποντας is 'urging' (exhorting), not 'turning'; διά + accusative before εὐσέβειαν is causal ('because of'). 'Ambassadors' (πρεσβευσάντων) may echo 2 Corinthians 5:20 (ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύομεν), and 'their word ran most swiftly' may echo Psalm 147:15 English (Psalm 147:4 LXX, ἕως τάχους δραμεῖται ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ) or 2 Thessalonians 3:1; possible allusions only, not cited inline. 'The power within it' keeps the singular ἐν αὐτῷ, which points ahead to 'the word'. 'Word' is capitalised where Origen moves from the apostles' word to the Word of God, who acts 'according to his own will'.
προτρέποντας: 'turning whole multitudes' -> 'urging whole multitudes ... to pass from' (exhort, not convert)
διὰ τὴν ... εὐσέβειαν: 'for the sake of' -> 'because of'; φανεῖσαν 'shone forth' -> 'shown itself'
Added 'But' for the contrasting δέ before 'the demonstration'
ὀξύτατα: 'speed and force' -> 'speed and keenness' ('force' was not in the Greek)
'even by punishing them' -> 'not even by punishing them'
Checked 1 Corinthians 2:4 against the verse; possible echoes (2 Corinthians 5:20, Psalm 147:15) rightly left uncited
